summary:
Most boards treat risk appetite as a policy document. It should be a decision tool. If your risk appetite statement cannot tell a front-line manager whether to take a specific deal or not, it is not doing its job.

Read the full article on our Insights page.

Climate transition is a governance issue before it is a reporting issue. Boards that wait for the disclosure mandate before engaging with transition risk are already behind.

Read more on our Insights page.

What does an actuarial board adviser actually do? It is not about checking the numbers. It is about making sure the board can interrogate the numbers -- and challenge the assumptions behind them.

Find out more on our Insights page.

AI governance in Singapore insurance: MAS has set clear expectations. What most boards are missing is not a policy -- it is the ability to ask the right questions of AI outputs before approving their use.

Read the full piece on our Insights page.

Capital strategy belongs in the boardroom -- not just in the actuarial report. Singapore insurance boards that leave capital decisions to management are not fulfilling their oversight duty under MAS Notice 126.

Read more at the link.

The ORSA is the most underused strategic tool available to Singapore insurance boards. Most firms treat it as a compliance exercise. The boards that use it properly get a live view of whether their capital can support their strategy.

Read the full article on our Insights page.

Cybersecurity Act 2026 makes cyber risk a board duty in Singapore -- not a CISO problem. Directors who cannot engage substantively with their organisation's cyber posture are now personally exposed.

Read what this means for boards at the link.

ESG compliance is not the same as ESG readiness. A board can tick every disclosure box and still have no coherent view of how sustainability risks affect the business model.

Read the full piece on our Insights page.

What five questions should every SGX audit committee ask the CRO? The answers reveal whether risk management is integrated into strategy or still sitting in a separate silo.

Read the full article at the link.

MAS Notice 126 creates personal accountability for Singapore insurance board directors. Most directors do not know exactly what they are accountable for -- until something goes wrong.

Read what the Notice actually requires at the link.

What does a board risk committee actually need to look like for a Singapore-listed company? Composition, mandate, MI, and the questions it should be asking every quarter.

Read the full piece on our Insights page.

Reinsurance strategy is a board decision -- not a technical one to be left entirely to the CRO or CFO. Singapore boards that do not understand their reinsurance programme cannot govern it.

Read more on our Insights page.

AI in reinsurance is not just a productivity story. It is an ecosystem transformation -- real-time risk exchange, parametric 2.0, AI-native MGAs. The reinsurers who treat it as a cost-reduction tool will be outpaced.

Read the full piece at the link.

Physical climate risk in Singapore insurance is no longer a scenario exercise. Boards need to understand how flood, heat, and storm tail risk sits inside their capital position -- not just in a disclosure appendix.

Read more at the link.

Indonesian insurance brokers now operate under POJK 44/2020, 4/2021 and 24/2023. ERM and BCP are no longer optional -- they are regulatory requirements with real consequences for firms that treat them as paperwork.
